title: Monohybrid cross. Interaction of allelic genes, multiple allelism. Di- and polyhybrid crosses. Interaction of non-allelic genes

goals.text: To teach the student the basic concepts and methods of genetics, G. Mendel’s laws and their cytological basis, the types of interaction of allelic and non-allelic genes, the inheritance of blood groups in humans and the method of solving genetic problems.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the basic terms of genetics (gene, allele, genotype, phenotype, homo- and heterozygote) and the rules of notation;
Mendel’s three laws and the hypothesis of gamete purity;
complete and incomplete dominance, codominance and multiple allelism;
the inheritance of blood groups in the ABO and Rh systems.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: solve problems on mono- and dihybrid crosses with a Punnett square;
determine the parental genotype from the result of a test cross;
calculate the probability of blood groups in children.

blocks.text: **Genetics** is the science of the laws of heredity and variability of organisms. Its founder is the Czech scientist **G. Mendel**, who announced the laws of inheritance in 1865 on the basis of his experiments with peas. These laws were rediscovered in 1900 by H. de Vries, C. Correns and E. Tschermak; the term “genetics” was introduced by W. Bateson in 1906. Later stages: T. Morgan’s chromosome theory, the DNA model of J. Watson and F. Crick (1953), the discovery of the genetic code, genetic engineering and the reading of the human genome (2003).

blocks.title: Table 4.1. Basic terms of genetics
head: Term
Definition
rows: A segment of DNA that determines the structure of a particular protein or RNA; the unit of heredity
The position of a gene on a chromosome
Genes located at the same loci of homologous chromosomes and determining different states of one trait (A and a)
A trait that appears (prevails) in the heterozygote — written with a capital letter (A)
A trait that appears only in the homozygote (aa) — written with a small letter

blocks.text: **Rules of notation:** P — parents, ♀ — female, ♂ — male, × — cross, G — gametes, F~1~, F~2~ — first and second generation hybrids. The female organism is written first. In human genetics the marriage of parents is also shown with “×”.

The main conditions of the **hybridological method** used by Mendel: pure lines (homozygotes) were chosen, clearly contrasting alternative traits were observed, and each generation was analyzed separately and quantitatively (statistically).

sections.title: 2. Monohybrid cross. Mendel’s first and second laws

blocks.text: A **monohybrid cross** is a cross of organisms that differ in one pair of alternative traits. When Mendel crossed yellow-seeded (AA) and green-seeded (aa) peas, all plants in F~1~ had yellow seeds (Aa); when F~1~ plants were crossed with each other, yellow and green seeds appeared in F~2~ in a 3 : 1 ratio (Figure 4.1).

blocks.label: Figure 4.1
blocks.caption: Mendel’s first and second laws shown in a Punnett square: crossing yellow (AA) and green (aa) peas, uniformity of F~1~ and segregation in F~2~ in a 3 : 1 ratio (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

items: **Mendel’s first law (law of uniformity of first-generation hybrids):** when two homozygous organisms differing in alternative traits are crossed, F~1~ hybrids are uniform in genotype and phenotype.

**Mendel’s second law (law of segregation):** when F~1~ heterozygotes are crossed with each other, traits segregate in F~2~ in a 3 : 1 ratio by phenotype and 1 : 2 : 1 by genotype (1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa).

blocks.text: **Hypothesis of gamete purity:** in a hybrid organism allelic genes do not blend; each gamete receives **only one allele** of the pair. Its **cytological basis** is the separation of homologous chromosomes (and the alleles on them) into different gametes in anaphase I of meiosis.

A **test cross** is crossing an organism with a dominant phenotype with a recessive homozygote (aa) to determine its genotype. If all offspring show the dominant trait, the organism tested is homozygous (AA); if segregation in a 1 : 1 ratio occurs, it is heterozygous (Aa).

parts.text: Problem-solving algorithm: (1) denote the traits with letters; (2) write the genotypes of the parents; (3) determine the gametes of each (each gamete carries one allele of each gene); (4) draw the Punnett square; (5) calculate the genotype and phenotype ratio or the probability (%).

sections.title: 3. Interaction of allelic genes and multiple allelism

blocks.text: **Multiple allelism** is the presence of more than two alleles at one locus in a population, though each organism carries only two of them. In humans the **ABO blood groups** are determined by the alleles I^0^, I^A^ and I^B^: I^A^ and I^B^ are dominant over I^0^ and codominant with each other.

blocks.title: Table 4.3. Genotypes of blood groups in the ABO system
head: Blood group
Antigen on erythrocytes
Antibody in plasma
Genotype

blocks.text: The **Rhesus factor** is determined by one main gene: Rh-positive (D — dominant) and Rh-negative (dd). If an Rh-negative mother carries an Rh-positive fetus, **Rh incompatibility** (hemolytic disease of the newborn) may develop in the second and later pregnancies.

parts.text: Blood group genetics is used in forensic medicine to **exclude** paternity: for example, a mother with group I (0) cannot have a child with group IV (AB). But blood groups **cannot prove** paternity — DNA analysis is needed for that. In the **Bombay phenomenon**, under the action of an epistatic recessive gene (hh), a person carrying the I^A^ or I^B^ gene appears to be group I (0).

sections.title: 4. Di- and polyhybrid crosses. Mendel’s third law

blocks.text: A **dihybrid cross** is a cross of organisms that differ in two pairs of alternative traits. When Mendel crossed yellow smooth (AABB) and green wrinkled (aabb) peas, all F~1~ were yellow smooth (AaBb). The F~1~ hybrid forms 4 kinds of gametes (AB, Ab, aB, ab), and in F~2~ there are 16 combinations, 9 genotypes and 4 phenotypes in a 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 ratio (Figure 4.2).

blocks.label: Figure 4.2
blocks.caption: Mendel’s third law (independent inheritance of traits) in a Punnett square: 16 combinations and the 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 phenotype ratio in the cross AaBb × AaBb; the letters under each genotype show the phenotype — D dominant, R recessive — for the first and second trait (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: **Mendel’s third law (law of independent inheritance):** in a dihybrid cross, segregation for each pair of traits proceeds in a 3 : 1 ratio independently of the other pair, and genes combine in all possible combinations. The law holds only if the genes are located **on different pairs of chromosomes**. Its cytological basis is the independent separation of homologous pairs in metaphase I.
Independent assortment can be proved by a **test cross**: in the cross AaBb × aabb four phenotypes appear in a 1 : 1 : 1 : 1 ratio.

sections.title: 5. Interaction of non-allelic genes and pleiotropy

blocks.title: Table 4.5. Interaction of non-allelic genes
head: Type
Essence
Ratio in F~2~
Example
rows: Two dominant non-allelic genes together produce a new trait
Normal hearing in humans: D_E_ (D — cochlea, E — development of the auditory nerve)
The dominant allele of one gene suppresses the expression of another (hypostatic) gene
Plumage color in chickens (gene I suppresses color)
A recessive homozygote (aa) suppresses the action of another gene

blocks.text: **Pleiotropy** is the effect of one gene on several traits. For example, in **Marfan syndrome** a mutation of the gene for the connective tissue protein fibrillin causes long “spider fingers”, dislocation of the lens and aortic aneurysm together; the **phenylketonuria** gene causes intellectual disability, light skin and hair and a peculiar odor of the urine.

parts.text: If the ratio adds up to **16**, a dihybrid cross (two genes) is involved: 9 + 7, 13 + 3, 12 + 3 + 1, 9 + 3 + 4, 15 + 1 are all “merged” variants of 9 : 3 : 3 : 1.

The expression of a gene is described by **penetrance** (the percentage of gene carriers in whom the trait appears) and **expressivity** (the degree to which the trait is expressed). For example, the polydactyly gene has incomplete penetrance.

skills.title: Skill: solving a dihybrid cross problem

items: Denote the traits: A — brown eyes, a — blue eyes; B — right-handedness, b — left-handedness.
Determine the parents’ genotypes from their phenotypes and the information about the children (if a child has a recessive trait, each parent carries the recessive allele of that gene).
Write the gametes of each parent (AaBb → AB, Ab, aB, ab).
Draw the Punnett square: horizontally — ♂ gametes, vertically — ♀ gametes.
Sort the genotypes in the squares into phenotypes and count them.
Write the answer as a ratio and a percentage (for example, the probability of a child with both recessive traits is 1/16 = 6.25 %).

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: In humans curly hair (A) is dominant over straight hair (a). A heterozygous curly-haired man married a straight-haired woman.
cases.ask: What genotypes and phenotypes are possible in the children? What is the probability of a straight-haired child?
cases.answer: P: ♀ aa × ♂ Aa. The woman’s gamete is a; the man’s are A and a. F~1~: Aa (curly) and aa (straight) in a 1 : 1 ratio. Thus the probability of a straight-haired child is 50 % (this is an example of a test cross).

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: Wilson disease (disorder of copper metabolism) is inherited as an autosomal recessive trait. One parent is ill; the other is healthy and has healthy parents, but this parent’s brother has Wilson disease.
cases.ask: Determine the probability of an affected child in this family.
cases.answer: The affected parent is aa. The healthy parent comes from healthy parents who have an affected son, so their parents are Aa × Aa, and the healthy parent, being unaffected, is AA (1/3) or Aa (2/3). If he or she is Aa, the probability of an affected child in the marriage aa × Aa is 1/2. Overall probability: 2/3 × 1/2 = 1/3 (≈ 33 %). If the healthy partner is known to be heterozygous — 50 %, if homozygous — 0 %.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: In humans brown eyes (A) are dominant over blue eyes (a), and nearsightedness — myopia (B) over normal vision (b). A blue-eyed myopic woman married a brown-eyed man with normal vision, and a blue-eyed child with normal vision was born.
cases.ask: Determine the genotypes of the parents and the probability of a brown-eyed myopic child in this family.
cases.answer: The child is aabb, so each parent gave the a and b alleles: the woman is aaBb, the man Aabb. Gametes: woman — aB, ab; man — Ab, ab. Children: AaBb (brown-eyed myopic), Aabb (brown-eyed normal), aaBb (blue-eyed myopic), aabb (blue-eyed normal) — each 1/4. The probability of a brown-eyed myopic child is 25 %.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: A gamete receives **only one allele** of each gene; an organism heterozygous for n gene pairs forms **2^n^** kinds of gametes.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Mendel’s laws: **“Uniform — Segregate — Independent”** (I — uniformity, II — segregation, III — independent inheritance).

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: ABO and Rh genetics is used in blood transfusion, prevention of Rh incompatibility and forensic exclusion of paternity.
